extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policy-makers in science of science, scientometrics, grant administrators, and those studying grant evaluation and scholarly communication
extracted.subtask_description: Quantitative analysis of how promotional (hype) language in grant proposals relates to funding success, measured innovativeness, and future citation/productivity impact; includes lexicon validation, robustness checks, and computer-assisted substitution experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of promotional words in a grant proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalized as a grant proposal’s total occurrences of promotional words ÷ a grant proposal’s total number of words (reported densities: median ≈1 promotion word per 100 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses a validated 139-word science-specific lexicon (see lexicon entry). Density is measured across the full text and observed to be higher in the first and last 500 words. Used as the primary predictor variable in regressions (logit/OLS/Negative Binomial) of funding, innovativeness, and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding success (binary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding success is coded as a binary variable (yes/no) indicating whether the grant was awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary dependent variable in logistic (logit) regression models. Models report effect sizes (e.g., a 1 percentage point increase in promotional words associated with ~46% increase in odds in NNF; significance levels provided). Regression specifications include extensive controls and fixed effects (see controls entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant innovativeness score (novelty index)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured using a validated novelty index that quantifies the degree to which a grant combines past knowledge in conventional or novel ways based on historical referencing patterns (journal-pair co-citation z-scores; proposal’s innovativeness = median of its negative z-scores; reverse-coded so larger = more innovative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires bibliographic/reference data. Less innovative proposals have journal pairs commonly co-cited historically (z > 0); innovative proposals have journal pairs that co-occur less than chance (z < 0). Used as an OLS outcome variable; reported effect (e.g., each 1 percentage point increase in promotional language associated with 1.4-point increase in innovativeness). SI Appendix contains computational details and example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future impact of grant-supported publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantified as (i) average journal impact factor (avg JIF) across publications acknowledging the grant, (ii) the largest JIF among those publications, and (iii) productivity measured as the number of publications supported by the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used OLS and Negative Binomial regressions controlling for grant amount and other confounds. JIFs are sometimes normalized by discipline (UCSD map of science) and used as proxies for expected citations when citation windows are immature. Reported associations: strong positive relation between promotional language and avg/max JIF (p < 0.001); weaker but significant relation with productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional words lexicon (139 science-specific words)
rubrics_metrics.description: A curated list of 139 science-specific 'promotional' or 'hype' words (e.g., compelling, critical, unique, groundbreaking, novel, revolutionary, transformative, promising, outstanding, etc.) originally created by Millar et al. (2022) and used here as the basis for counting promotional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Millar et al.’s manual process reviewed each candidate word in ≥500 contexts and evaluated substitutability with a neutral synonym (reported Cohen’s k = 0.82). The paper lists example words and reports the full lexicon; researchers should use the same dictionary for replication or apply equivalent validation if modifying the lexicon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexicon validation and psychometric checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Three independent validation checks on the 139-word lexicon: (i) multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) external validation comparing valence/arousal to neutral synonyms, (ii) internal consistency via Cronbach’s alpha (NNF=0.57, NSF=0.53, NIH=0.63), and (iii) correlation of individual word frequencies with total promotional-word frequency (88% correlated at p < 0.01).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where words showed weaker properties (remaining 12%), separate analyses using only the 88% subset were run and found no statistical difference from main findings. The paper reports significance tests (p-values) and advises addressing problematic words by sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment estimation via SciBert (positive sentiment score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence-level sentiment estimated with SciBert (a domain-specific contextual embedding model) fine-tuned on manually labeled grant sentences; model outputs confidence scores for positive/neutral/negative labels and the analysis focuses on the positive sentiment score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine-tuning used 1,021 manually coded sentences from NSF/NIH abstracts with three raters; pairwise agreement and Cohen’s kappa reported; SciBert achieved F1 ≈ 0.79 on the full fine-tuning set. Use of a domain-specific model and in-domain fine-tuning is recommended for reliable sentiment estimation in scientific text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental substitution procedure (promotional → neutral synonyms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-assisted experiments replaced promotional words with randomly chosen neutral synonyms (sourced from Oxford Dictionary and human-reviewed for scientific context) at substitution levels of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%, repeating random substitutions 100 times per proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After substitutions, SciBert-estimated positive sentiment compared between original and replica proposals; statistical test per proposal: binomial test over 100 trials (K = trials where original > replica). Across datasets, substituting promotional words leads to significant drops in positive sentiment (e.g., >88% of NIH/NSF proposals show sentiment decrease when 100% substituted). Details and synonym lists are in SI Appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression model covariates and fixed effects (control variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regression specifications control for PI characteristics (self-reported demographics, prior productivity and citation impact, prior grant application and success), grant features (writing style, readability, length, applied/funded amount), and fixed effects for year, grant type, program area/domain specializations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models report BIC, VIF, cross-validation, and other diagnostics (see SI Appendix, Table S1 and Section II). Inclusion of these confounds is necessary to isolate the unique role of promotional language; researchers should pre-specify similar controls when replicating analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks for measurement error and specification sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Three robustness approaches: (i) count each unique promotional word only once per proposal, (ii) randomly drop up to 20% of a proposal’s promotional words (100 repetitions), (iii) randomly drop 5%–20% of words from the promotional dictionary (100 repetitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These robustness tests showed results remain significant (though p-values fall as measurement error increases); promotional words continued to predict funding at p < 0.05 under these perturbations. The paper recommends running similar perturbation analyses to gauge sensitivity to lexicon/context misclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sampling and representativeness criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets include full text of both funded and unfunded grant proposals from three funders: NNF (13,520 proposals, 2015–2022), NIH (2,649), NSF (561) — with deidentified PI data (age, gender, publication/citation records) and proposal metadata (year, program area, applied/funded amounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors emphasize inclusion of unfunded proposals to mitigate selection bias and report average lengths, award sizes, and funding rates for the samples. Data access for replication requires NDA processes for funder data (NNF, University NDA for NIH/NSF). Use of both funded and unfunded full-text proposals is recommended to avoid selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of statistical associations and interpretation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect sizes, confidence intervals, and p-values are reported for associations between promotional language and outcomes (e.g., funding probability, innovativeness, avg/max JIF, productivity); model selection metrics (BIC) used to compare models (e.g., promotional-word-only model had lowest BIC vs. sentiment-only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors caution about causality vs. correlation, discuss potential mechanisms (e.g., promotional words increase positive impressions/cognitive activation), and recommend experimental or quasi-experimental designs (the substitution experiment is one such approach) to probe causal pathways. They also note domain-specificity: findings may be grant-specific and not generalize to papers/patents without further study.
